deep.reconstruction:
This page is a printed page (p. 80) of an 18th-century German arithmetic and algebra textbook in Fraktur. The copy is interleaved, and Gauss wrote notes on the blank interleaved leaves. The printed text contains no derivation. It continues §170, the start of the 'Vierter Abschnitt: Von den algebraischen Gleichungen', with the following content.

(i) Basic definitions of equation solving:
- The 'Fundamental-Gleichung' is the first equation, obtained by writing the given conditions in letters.
- Further equations are derived from it using the book's §§8, 17, 55, i.e. the rules for transforming equations.
- These lead to the 'Endgleichung' x = (expression in known quantities only), and the equation is then 'aufgelöset'.

(ii) The Anmerkung:
- It divides analysis into 'gemeine' (common) analysis, covering determinate equations of degree at most 2, and 'höhere' (higher) analysis.
- Higher analysis covers determinate equations of higher degree and indeterminate equations, with constant or variable values and of determinate or indeterminate degree.
- Variable quantities of determinate degree are called algebraic; those of indeterminate degree are called transcendental. Where the exponents are themselves variable they are exponential quantities. Values of variable quantities in general are called functions.
- It sketches the history of the calculus: Newton (prompted by Barrow), simultaneously Leibniz, then the Bernoullis, de l'Hôpital and Euler.

(iii) §171 begins: an equation is determinate if its value can be given by known quantities, and indeterminate otherwise. The catchword is '4 x'.

The only Gauss material visible is the cut-off left edges of notes on the facing interleaved leaf: '(x^m+', '= x', 'si', 'x', 'φx', 'A'=', 'A''=', 'A'''=', an integral sign or long s, 'φx =', 'd… in…'. These are the beginnings of the notes fully transcribed on the next page. They contain two results:

(a) A formula for a power of a gapped power series:
(x^m + (1)x^{m+δ} + (2)x^{m+2δ} + …)^t = x^{mt} Σ x^{sδ} · [t(t−1)…(t−n+1) / ((I)! (II)! (III)! …)] · (1)^{(I)} (2)^{(II)} (3)^{(III)} …
The sum runs over (I)+2(II)+3(III)+… = s, with n = (I)+(II)+(III)+…. This is the multinomial (Arbogast/de Moivre type) coefficient formula for a power of a series.

(b) The Lagrange inversion series. If x = t + uX, then φ(x) = Σ (u^n/n!) d^{n−1}/dt^{n−1}[X^n φ'(t)]. It is derived by Taylor expansion in u with coefficients A', A'', A''', and ends with 'Die gewöhnliche Form des Lehrsatzes' ('the usual form of the theorem').

Nothing on this page itself can be reconstructed beyond these fragments.
errors: No mathematical errors in the printed text; it is definitional and historical.
The claim that 'common' analysis is limited to equations not exceeding degree 2 is a textbook convention, not a mathematical statement.
The margin fragments are too truncated on this page to check; their full versions (next page) appear consistent with Lagrange's series.

results.what: Printed textbook definitions: fundamental equation, end equation, solved equation, determinate vs indeterminate equation; classification of algebraic, transcendental and exponential quantities and functions; history of the calculus.
Marginal fragment (continued on next page): power of a power series with multinomial coefficients.
results.modern_name: Multinomial theorem for powers of a power series

results.what: Marginal fragment (continued on next page): expansion of φ(x) with x = t + uX(x) via coefficients A', A'', A'''.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed textbook page with routine definitions and history. The only Gauss content is truncated margin fragments of a standard derivation of Lagrange's inversion series and the multinomial expansion. Gauss is known to have used both, and they appear in full on the next page.

transcription_corrections: The page body is printed Fraktur text, not Gauss's handwriting; the transcription of the printed text is essentially correct.

The right-margin items ('(x^m+', 'A'=', 'A''=', 'A'''=', 'φx =', etc.) are the cut-off left edges of the handwritten notes on the facing interleaved leaf, transcribed in full as the next page. 'si' is Latin 'si' (if), introducing the condition (I)+2(II)+3(III)+…=s.
The fragment read as '∫ [?]' is more likely part of a long s or a ∂ symbol from the next-page notes than an integral sign.
